text: William Hodgson "Hod" Stuart (February 20, 1879 – June 23, 1907) was a Canadian professional ice hockey player who played as a cover-point (now known as a defenceman) for nine seasons from 1899 to 1907 across various leagues. He also briefly played Canadian football for the Ottawa Rough Riders. With his brother Bruce, Stuart was a key player in the first professional ice hockey league, the American-based International Professional Hockey League (IPHL), where he was considered one of the best players. Frustrated by the violence in the IPHL, he left the league in late 1906 and returned to Canada, where in 1907 he helped the Montreal Wanderers win the Stanley Cup. Two months later, he died in a diving accident near Belleville, Ontario, after swimming to a lighthouse and diving headfirst into shallow, jagged rocks, which gashed his head and broke his neck. To support his widow and two children, the Eastern Canada Amateur Hockey Association hosted an all-star game, the first of its kind in any sport, on January 2, 1908, which drew an estimated 3,800 spectators and was described by the Montreal Herald as "unique in the history of hockey in Montreal, if not in the whole of Canada." The event, held at Westmount Arena for no charge, raised over $2,100 for Stuart’s family, with all proceeds going to his family. Stuart was known for his ability to score goals while playing a defensive role, his calm demeanor during violent games, and his efforts to reduce violence and increase player salaries. These contributions were recognized when he was one of the first nine players inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame in 1945, and his brother Bruce was inducted in 1961. Born in Ottawa, Ontario, the eldest son of William Stuart and Rachel Hodgson, he had two brothers (Alex and Bruce) and two sisters (Jessie and Lottio). From an early age, he played hockey with his brother Bruce, as well as rugby and football, and played for the Ottawa Rough Riders. He also worked as a bricklayer and later in construction with his father. He was described as quiet and rarely spoke about his achievements except with close friends. He married Loughlin around 1903, and they had two children. Stuart began his senior hockey career with the Rat Portage Thistles in 1895–1896, then joined the Ottawa Hockey Club in the Canadian Amateur Hockey League (CAHL) in 1899, captained the team in 1900, and moved to Quebec in 1900 to join the Quebec Bulldogs, where he scored seven goals in fifteen games over two seasons. In 1902, he signed with the Pittsburgh Bankers of the Western Pennsylvania Hockey League, winning a dispute with the Pittsburgh Victorias, and earned a salary of US$15–20 per week plus a day job. He scored seven goals and had eight assists in 1903 and was named the best cover-point in the league. He then played for the Portage Lakes Hockey Club in 1903–1904, scoring thirteen goals in fourteen exhibition games, and joined the Calumet Miners in the IPHL, where he scored eighteen goals in 1904–1905, helped the team win the league championship, and was named best cover-point on the all-star team. On December 11, 1905, he was suspended for being too rough and winning too many championships, but was reinstated on December 30 and joined the Pittsburgh Professionals. After the season, he played one game with Calumet in a bid to win the league title, which they lost, and was again named best cover-point after scoring eleven goals. He was considered the finest defenceman of his era for his offensive and defensive skills. In December 1906, he published a letter in the Montreal Star criticizing the IPHL's officiating, stating the referees were "dumb and incompetent," and after Pittsburgh refused to play against Michigan Soo due to a referee dispute, he was released. He then joined the Montreal Wanderers, whose first game with him drew 6,069 fans, one of the largest audiences for a hockey game in Canada at the time. He participated in the Wanderers' Stanley Cup challenge against the New Glasgow Cubs, becoming one of the first professional players to compete for the Cup. Despite violence during games—such as when Alf Smith hit him across the temple and Charles Spittal attempted to split Cecil Blachford's skull—he remained calm and did not retaliate, earning praise for his composure. The Montreal Victorias proposed suspending the offending players, but the vote failed and the league president resigned; later, Spittal and Alf Smith were fined $20 after being arrested. Despite the violence, Stuart helped the Wanderers go undefeated and win the Stanley Cup after defeating the Kenora Thistles in a rematch. Though he did not score in any of the four games, he played his best game of his career in the first match of the series with a broken finger. He was regarded as the most important player on the team and known for his knowledge of all positions and his ability to pass that knowledge to teammates. After the 1907 Stanley Cup victory, he quit hockey and joined his father in construction, overseeing the building of the Belleville Drill Shed. While in Belleville, he received offers to manage teams in Belleville, Peterborough, and a team outside Toronto that offered a railroad president's salary. On June 23, 1907, he died in the diving accident. His funeral in Ottawa was attended by representatives from the Ottawa Hockey Club, Ottawa Rowing Club, Ottawa Football Club, St. Patrick's Football Club, Ottawa Victorias, and Montreal Wanderers, along with family, friends, and city aldermen. James Strachan, president of the Montreal Wanderers, called him "a splendid hockey player, and one of the finest fellows in the game," and Billy Strachan, a teammate, said he had a high opinion of him as a player and a man. Lorne Campbell, a teammate, stated that Stuart was the best cover-point in the game's history and helped revolutionize the role of the puck-rushing defenceman. Campbell noted that despite appearing slow due to his skating style, Stuart was the speediest player of his size, had excellent stickhandling and long reach, and was one of the best generals in the game. He was not a violent player, but rather "more sinned against than sinning," and had to use a specially padded glove due to repeated stick whacks to his hands.
